claim: Antibodies are used in many areas of biomedical and clinical research.
source: Antibodies are used in many areas of biomedical and clinical research, but many of these antibodies have not been adequately characterized, which casts doubt on the results reported in many scientific papers.
evidence: This is a general statement about the use of antibodies in research, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Many antibodies used in biomedical and clinical research have not been adequately characterized.
source: Antibodies are used in many areas of biomedical and clinical research, but many of these antibodies have not been adequately characterized, which casts doubt on the results reported in many scientific papers.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations and data throughout the manuscript discussing the antibody characterization crisis.

claim: Inadequate antibody characterization casts doubt on the results reported in many scientific papers.
source: Antibodies are used in many areas of biomedical and clinical research, but many of these antibodies have not been adequately characterized, which casts doubt on the results reported in many scientific papers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the logical consequence of using poorly characterized antibodies in research.

claim: A lack of suitable control experiments in many studies compounds the antibody characterization problem.
source: This problem is compounded by a lack of suitable control experiments in many studies.
evidence: This is stated as a contributing factor to the antibody crisis and is supported by discussions throughout the manuscript.

claim: The antibody market has grown from approximately 10,000 commercially available antibodies about 15 years ago to more than six million today.
source: For these reasons, the market for antibodies has soared, growing from ~10,000 commercially available antibodies about 15 years ago, to more than six million today (Longworth and Chalmers, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Longworth and Chalmers, 2022.

claim: Approximately 50% of commercial antibodies fail to meet even basic standards for characterization.
source: However, it has been estimated that ~50% of commercial antibodies fail to meet even basic standards for characterization, and this problem is thought to result in financial losses of $0.4–1.8 billion per year in the United States alone (Ayoubi et al., 2023; Bradbury and Plückthun, 2015; Voskuil et al., 2020; Baker, 2015b).
evidence: This estimate is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The problem of inadequate antibody characterization results in financial losses of $0.4–1.8 billion per year in the United States alone.
source: However, it has been estimated that ~50% of commercial antibodies fail to meet even basic standards for characterization, and this problem is thought to result in financial losses of $0.4–1.8 billion per year in the United States alone (Ayoubi et al., 2023; Bradbury and Plückthun, 2015; Voskuil et al., 2020; Baker, 2015b).
evidence: This financial estimate is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Problems caused by variable quality and characterization of commercial antibodies are compounded by end users not receiving sufficient training in the identification and use of suitable antibodies.
source: Moreover, the problems caused by the variable quality and characterization of commercial antibodies are compounded by end users not receiving sufficient training in the identification and use of suitable antibodies.
evidence: This is stated as a contributing factor to the antibody crisis.

claim: There has been an alarming increase in the number of scientific publications that contain misleading or incorrect interpretations and conclusions because they are based on data from experiments that used antibodies that had not been properly characterized or validated.
source: Together these issues have led to an alarming increase in the number of scientific publications that contain misleading or incorrect interpretations and conclusions because they are based on data from experiments that used antibodies that had not been properly characterized or validated (Goodman, 2018; Menke et al., 2020; Laflamme et al., 2019; Aponte Santiago et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations documenting the problem.

claim: There is a growing body of data that includes stark demonstrations of the volume of incorrect or misleading data published, including clinical patient trials, based upon the use of poorly characterized antibodies.
source: There is also a growing body of data that includes stark demonstrations of the volume of incorrect or misleading data published, including clinical patient trials (see, for example, Andersson et al., 2017, Virk et al., 2019, and table 1 in Voskuil et al., 2020), based upon the use of poorly characterized antibodies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific examples.

claim: Therapeutic antibodies are very well regulated and are subject to strict controls involving manufacturer and clinical trials.
source: (It should be noted, however, that therapeutic antibodies – unlike research antibodies – are very well regulated and are subject to strict controls involving manufacturer and clinical trials; Longworth and Chalmers, 2022).
evidence: This claim distinguishes therapeutic antibodies from research antibodies and is supported by a citation.

claim: The roots of the antibody characterization problem can be traced back to the early 2000s, when the first near-complete human genome sequence became available.
source: The roots of this now pervasive problem can be traced back to the early 2000 s, when the first near-complete human genome sequence became available, and attention turned to using this information to make further discoveries in biomedical sciences.
evidence: This provides historical context for the antibody crisis.

claim: The Human Proteome Organization was formed in response to open questions about how many proteins are encoded in the human genome and which are expressed in different tissues.
source: Analyses of the genome resulted in open questions as to how many proteins are encoded and which are expressed in different tissues. Such discussions resulted in formation of the Human Proteome Organization (Omenn, 2021) and its Human Proteome Project (Legrain et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Omenn, 2021 and Legrain et al., 2011.

claim: The Human Proteome Project focused on the determination of the human proteome based upon experimental evidence and the development of tools (notably mass spectrometry and antibodies) to enable further research.
source: As suggested by the name, the Human Proteome Project focused on the determination of the human proteome, based upon experimental evidence, and the development of tools (notably mass spectrometry and antibodies) to enable further research.
evidence: This describes the goals of the Human Proteome Project.

claim: The Human Proteome Project developed three foundational approaches to determine the human proteome: shotgun and targeted mass spectrometry, polyclonal and monoclonal antibodies, and an integrated database.
source: They also developed three foundational approaches to determine the human proteome and make it available to researchers: (i) shotgun and targeted mass spectrometry; (ii) polyclonal and monoclonal antibodies; (iii) an integrated database, intended to promote sharing of data and a platform for multiple uses.
evidence: This describes the specific approaches used by the Human Proteome Project.

claim: The Human Protein Atlas was launched around the same time as the Human Proteome Project and had similar goals: to map all human proteins in cells, tissues, and organs.
source: The Human Protein Atlas was launched around the same time and had similar goals: to map all human proteins in cells, tissues, and organs. This project's approach was highly dependent upon use of antibodies in immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence (Berglund et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Berglund et al., 2008.

claim: The Human Protein Atlas project's approach was highly dependent upon use of antibodies in immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence.
source: The Human Protein Atlas was launched around the same time and had similar goals: to map all human proteins in cells, tissues, and organs. This project's approach was highly dependent upon use of antibodies in immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence (Berglund et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Berglund et al., 2008.

claim: The costs associated with performing basic antibody characterizations and obtaining appropriate knockout cell lines are many times higher than the revenues generated from the average antibody on the market today.
source: It is important for anyone hoping to understand and address the antibody crisis to realise that the costs associated with performing even the most basic/common characterizations (Western blotting, immunoprecipitation, immunofluorescence and immunohistochemistry), and obtaining appropriate knockout cell lines, is many times higher than the revenues generated from the average antibody on the market today.
evidence: This is stated as an economic reality that explains why vendors do not routinely characterize antibodies.

claim: The current system puts the onus on end users to both find the best antibody on the market for them and to perform appropriate characterization prior to using the antibody.
source: Thus, the current system puts the onus on end users to both find the best antibody on the market for them, and to perform appropriate characterization prior to using the antibody – otherwise they could waste a lot of time and money on experiments that do not produce meaningful or trustworthy results.
evidence: This describes the current state of responsibility in antibody use.

claim: The research community is failing to take advantage of all the information contained in the human genome sequence because the high-quality reagents (including antibodies) needed to investigate a large fraction of the proteome are simply not available or identifiable as a result of the lack of characterization data linked to them.
source: A related issue is that with the focus placed on the most widely used antibodies, the research community is failing to take advantage of all the information contained in the human genome sequence because the high-quality reagents (including antibodies) needed to investigate a large fraction of the proteome are simply not available or identifiable as a result of the lack of characterization data linked to them (Edwards et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Edwards et al., 2011.

claim: The term antibody 'characterization' is more apt than 'validation', as an antibody's suitability often varies across different assays.
source: The term antibody 'characterization' is more apt than 'validation', as an antibody's suitability often varies across different assays.
evidence: This is a definitional claim about terminology in the field.

claim: Antibody characterization describes the inherent ability of an antibody to perform in different assays.
source: The term antibody 'characterization' is best applied to a description of the inherent ability of an antibody to perform in different assays – i.e. for a recombinant antibody it describes the properties of an antibody with a specific sequence (e.g. functional in Western blot, immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence, but not in immunoprecipitation).
evidence: This is a definitional claim about the term 'characterization'.

claim: Validation is best applied to confirmation that a particular antibody lot received in a lab performs as characterized.
source: While validation is best applied to confirmation that a particular antibody lot received in a lab performs as characterized – an antibody may not be validated if (for example) it has been inadvertently denatured by environmental extremes.
evidence: This is a definitional claim about the term 'validation'.

claim: Polyclonal antibodies are a large source of the problems in antibody characterization due to their non-renewable nature and the complexity of the different antibodies present.
source: The prevalent use of polyclonal antibodies, derived from immunized animals and most often used in the form of serum from such animals, is a large source of the problems described herein. This is due to their non-renewable nature and the complexity of the different antibodies present, which can influence batch variability as a result of the presence of both specific and non-specific antibodies.
evidence: This explains why polyclonal antibodies are problematic.

claim: Polyclonal antibodies may introduce false positives and increased background noise.
source: This may introduce false positives and increased background noise, and is further confounded when serum from different bleeds or animals is sold under the same name and catalog number.
evidence: This describes specific problems with polyclonal antibodies.

claim: The profile of a polyclonal antibody response can vary over time, even with affinity purification, as the antibody population in each batch is varied.
source: Also, the profile of a polyclonal antibody response can vary over time, even with affinity purification, as the antibody population in each batch is varied.
evidence: This describes batch-to-batch variability in polyclonal antibodies.

claim: Monoclonal antibodies were the first type of renewable antibody as they could be generated repeatedly and would remain consistent.
source: Thus, monoclonal antibodies were the first type of renewable antibody as they could be generated repeatedly and would remain consistent.
evidence: This is a historical statement about monoclonal antibodies.

claim: Hybridoma lines can vary over time and may express more than one antibody.
source: However, caution is advised as hybridoma lines can vary over time and may express more than one antibody (Bradbury et al., 2018; Mitchell et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bradbury et al., 2018 and Mitchell et al., 2023.

claim: Recombinant antibodies offer stable and renewable reagents, with customizable constant regions for varied applications and much more flexibility in use.
source: This allows cloning it into plasmids to allow expression of a single antibody, offering stable and renewable reagents, with customizable constant regions for varied applications and much more flexibility in use.
evidence: This describes advantages of recombinant antibodies.

claim: In the early 2000s, researchers and journals began raising the alarm about the growing antibody crisis.
source: In the early 2000s, researchers and journals began raising the alarm about the growing antibody crisis, explaining why appropriate controls and detailed/accurate reporting of antibodies was so important (Saper, 2005; Saper, 2009; Saper and Sawchenko, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to early papers on the topic.

claim: Bordeaux et al. (2010) stressed the need to differentiate between the lack of antibody characterization and scientific misconduct or data manipulation.
source: In a review article titled 'Antibody Validation' that was published in 2010, Bordeaux and co-authors discussed the importance of antibody characterization in some detail (Bordeaux et al., 2010), while also stressing the need to differentiate between the lack of antibody characterization and scientific misconduct or data manipulation (Collins and Tabak, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bordeaux et al., 2010 and Collins and Tabak, 2014.

claim: Knockout or knockdown cell lines or tissue samples are important negative controls for antibody specificity.
source: Moreover, we encourage the use of knockout (KO) or knockdown (KD) cell lines or tissue samples as important negative controls for specificity.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on best practices in the field.

claim: KO cell lines and model organisms have become much more readily available, thanks to CRISPR technologies.
source: KO cell lines and model organisms have become much more readily available, thanks to CRISPR technologies, and the use of antibodies to confirm KO of a protein is just as useful a tool as the use of the KO lines to test for specificity of antibodies.
evidence: This is a statement about the impact of CRISPR technology on the availability of KO cell lines.

claim: There is currently no repository that researchers can use to share KO cell lines.
source: Unfortunately, there is currently no repository that researchers can use to share KO cell lines.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in available resources.

claim: The Global Biological Standards Institute (GBSI) was established in 2012.
source: The Global Biological Standards Institute (GBSI), established in 2012, played a significant role by forming a Research Antibodies and Standards Task Force, and its 2015 online survey and subsequent analyses (Freedman et al., 2016) emphasized the urgent need for better training for end users and for standards for best practices.
evidence: This is a historical fact about the founding of GBSI.

claim: A GBSI study found that the US spends approximately $28 billion per year on preclinical research that is not reproducible.
source: Another GBSI study found that the US spends ~$28 billion per year on preclinical research that is not reproducible, and concluded that urgent improvements were required in two areas – study design and the validation of biological reagents (Freedman et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Freedman et al., 2015.

claim: FASEB published a report called Enhancing Research Reproducibility in 2016, which stressed the need for standard reporting formats for antibodies.
source: The Federation of American Societies of Experimental Biology (FASEB) also published an important report called Enhancing Research Reproducibility in 2016, which stressed the need for standard reporting formats for antibodies (FASEB, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to FASEB, 2016.

claim: An ad hoc International Working Group for Antibody Validation was formed in 2016 with a goal of addressing the collective need for standards to validate antibody specificity and reproducibility.
source: An ad hoc International Working Group for Antibody Validation was formed in 2016 with a goal of addressing the "collective need for standards to validate antibody specificity and reproducibility, as well as the need for reporting practices" (Uhlen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Uhlen et al., 2016.

claim: The International Working Group for Antibody Validation introduced the 'five pillars' of antibody characterization: genetic strategies, orthogonal strategies, multiple (independent) antibody strategies, recombinant strategies, and immunocapture MS strategies.
source: This group introduced the 'five pillars' of antibody characterization (Table 1): (i) genetic strategies (i.e., the use of knockout and knockdown techniques as controls for specificity); (ii) orthogonal strategies (i.e., comparing the results of antibody-dependent and antibody-independent experiments); (iii) multiple (independent) antibody strategies (which compare the results of experiments that use different antibodies to target the same protein); (iv) recombinant strategies (which increase target protein expression); (v) immunocapture MS strategies (in which mass spectrometry is used to identify the protein(s) captured by the antibody).
evidence: This describes the five pillars framework introduced by the working group.

claim: The five pillars are not intended to encompass all useful characterization strategies, nor are they all required for each characterization effort.
source: These pillars are not intended to encompass all useful characterization strategies, nor are they all required for each characterization effort: rather, users are encouraged to use as many as feasible (Uhlen et al., 2016).
evidence: This clarifies the intended use of the five pillars framework, supported by citation to Uhlen et al., 2016.

claim: The Human Protein Atlas (HPA) was funded in 2003 by the Wallenberg Foundation.
source: The Human Protein Atlas (HPA), funded in 2003 by the Wallenberg Foundation, is based in Sweden.
evidence: This is a historical fact about the founding of HPA.

claim: The first reports generated by the HPA were in 2005 and included data from 718 antibodies.
source: The first reports generated by the HPA were in 2005 and included data from 718 antibodies generated both by the HPA and those obtained from commercial sources (Uhlén et al., 2005; Nilsson et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Uhlén et al., 2005 and Nilsson et al., 2005.

claim: NeuroMab is a facility at the University of California Davis with goals that include the generation of mouse monoclonal antibodies optimized for use in studies of mammalian brains.
source: NeuroMab is a facility at the University of California Davis, with goals that include the generation of mouse monoclonal antibodies – and, more recently, recombinant antibodies – optimized for use in studies of mammalian brains, with emphasis on antibodies useful in immunohistochemistry and Western Blots.
evidence: This describes the mission of NeuroMab.

claim: NeuroMab has been funded by the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke since 2005.
source: Funded by the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (which is part of NIH) since 2005, it works with researchers to identify targets relevant to brain studies, and to generate the optimal immunogen(s) and monoclonal antibodies that target them.
evidence: This is a historical fact about NeuroMab's funding.

claim: NeuroMab has generated antibodies directed towards more than 800 target proteins.
source: They have generated antibodies directed towards more than 800 target proteins, using their system of immunohistochemistry, Western Blots, and immunofluorescence characterization.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about NeuroMab's output.

claim: The NIH funded the Protein Capture Reagent Program (PCRP) for five years starting in 2010.
source: Concerted efforts toward the goals of a collection of monoclonal antibodies covering the human proteome ramped up dramatically in 2010 when the NIH funded the Protein Capture Reagent Program (PCRP) for five years.
evidence: This is a historical fact about the PCRP funding.

claim: The PCRP focused on the generation and characterization of monoclonal antibodies and recombinant antibodies targeting human transcription factors.
source: This program focused on the generation and characterization of monoclonal antibodies and recombinant antibodies targeting human transcription factors (Roy et al., 2021; Venkataraman et al., 2018; Lai et al., 2021; Blackshaw et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The PCRP produced a collection of 1406 monoclonal antibodies targeting 737 human proteins.
source: Among specific outputs from this program are a collection of 1406 monoclonal antibodies (available through the DSHB) targeting 737 human proteins (Venkataraman et al., 2018; Lai et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Venkataraman et al., 2018 and Lai et al., 2021.

claim: The Affinomics program was funded by the EU.
source: The EU-funded Affinomics program grew out of two earlier projects: ProteomeBinders (Taussig et al., 2007) and AffinityProteome (Stoevesandt and Taussig, 2012a).
evidence: This is a historical fact about Affinomics funding.

claim: The 286 antibodies generated by Affinomics have been shared and are available through the DSHB.
source: The 286 antibodies generated have been shared and are available through the DSHB.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about Affinomics output.

claim: CiteAb began as a data mining research project in the laboratory of Andrew Chalmers at the University of Bath in 2012.
source: It began as a data mining research project in the laboratory of Andrew Chalmers at the University of Bath in 2012.
evidence: This is a historical fact about CiteAb's origins.

claim: CiteAb today covers over 14 million reagents with links to 6 million citations.
source: Through data mining coupled with manual reviewing of the literature and collaborations with vendors of antibodies, it quickly grew and today covers over 14 million reagents with links to 6 million citations.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about CiteAb's current scope.

claim: The Research Resource Identifier (RRID) program can generate unique identifiers for antibodies and other reagents.
source: The Research Resource Identifier (RRID) program can generate unique identifiers for antibodies and other reagents (Menke et al., 2020; Bandrowski et al., 2016; Bandrowski et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: An antibody can be sold by multiple different vendors with each using a different RRID number.
source: It is also important to note that an antibody can be sold by multiple different vendors with each using a different RRID number, and different lots of the same manufacturer's antibody will have the same RRID, even if there may be significant lot-to-lot variation.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the RRID system.

claim: By 2017, more than 5,000 articles in more than 380 journals were including RRID data.
source: By 2017 >5,000 articles in >380 journals were including RRID data and today those numbers are much higher.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about RRID adoption.

claim: The Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank (DSHB) was established in 1986.
source: Since its inception in 1986, the Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank (DSHB) at the University of Iowa has maintained and distributed at minimal cost hybridoma cell lines and monoclonal antibodies shared by investigators.
evidence: This is a historical fact about DSHB's founding.

claim: Over 6,000 hybridoma lines are maintained by DSHB.
source: Over 6,000 hybridoma lines – including those submitted by the PCRP, Affinomics, CPTAC, and NeuroMab initiatives – are maintained by DSHB, which also manages more than 600 recombinant antibodies, many of which come from the CPTAC.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about DSHB's holdings.

claim: DSHB distributed more than 65,000 samples in the past year.
source: With >65,000 samples distributed in the past year, the DSHB remains an important component in the availability of research antibodies.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about DSHB's distribution activity.

claim: DSHB has been fully supported by user fees since 1997.
source: DSHB was originally funded by the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (which is part of NIH), but it has been fully supported by user fees since 1997.
evidence: This is a historical fact about DSHB's funding model.

claim: The National Cancer Institute set up the Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) in 2006.
source: The National Cancer Institute (part of the NIH) set up the Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) in 2006 to fund both intramural and extramural projects.
evidence: This is a historical fact about CPTAC's founding.

claim: The CPTAC Antibody Characterization Laboratory has developed 946 antibodies targeting 570 antigens.
source: At the time of writing, the ACL has developed 946 antibodies targeting 570 antigens (proteomics.cancer.gov/antibody-portal), which are obtainable from the DSHB.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about ACL's output.

claim: The Antibody Characterization through Open Science (YCharOS) initiative was launched in 2020 at the Montreal Neurological Institute at McGill University as part of the SGC.
source: In 2020 the Antibody Characterization through Open Science, or YCharOS initiative, was launched at the Montreal Neurological Institute at McGill University as part of the SGC, with a focus on the characterization of existing antibodies.
evidence: This is a historical fact about YCharOS's founding.

claim: As of March 2023, YCharOS has reported results from the testing of more than 1,000 antibodies and had published 96 antibody characterization reports.
source: As of March 2023, YCharOS has reported results from the testing of more than 1,000 antibodies and had published 96 antibody characterization reports (one report per protein) at zenodo.org/communities/ycharos, and a number of peer-reviewed articles at f1000research.com/ycharos.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about YCharOS's output.

claim: A YCharOS study analyzed a set of 614 antibodies targeting 65 proteins.
source: The YCharOS group recently published a highly impactful study that analyzed a set of 614 antibodies targeting 65 proteins (Ayoubi et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ayoubi et al., 2023.

claim: The YCharOS study found that 50–75% of the protein set was covered by at least one high-performing commercial antibody, depending on the application.
source: For example, the group found that 50–75% of the protein set was covered by at least one high-performing commercial antibody, depending on the application.
evidence: This is a data-based finding from the YCharOS study.

claim: The YCharOS study showed the use of KO cell lines to be superior to other types of controls for Western Blots, and even more so for immunofluorescence imaging.
source: This study also showed the use of KO cell lines to be superior to other types of controls for Western Blots, and even more so for immunofluorescence imaging.
evidence: This is a finding from the YCharOS study comparing different control methods.

claim: The YCharOS study revealed that an average of approximately 12 publications per protein target included data from an antibody that failed to recognize the relevant target protein.
source: Shockingly, it also revealed that an average of ~12 publications per protein target included data from an antibody that failed to recognize the relevant target protein!
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the YCharOS study about the extent of the problem.

claim: Vendors proactively removed approximately 20% of the antibodies tested by YCharOS that failed to meet expectations.
source: These vendors proactively removed ~20% of the antibodies tested that failed to meet expectations, and modified the proposed applications for ~40% (Ayoubi et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about vendor responses to YCharOS data, supported by citation.

claim: Vendors modified the proposed applications for approximately 40% of the antibodies tested by YCharOS.
source: These vendors proactively removed ~20% of the antibodies tested that failed to meet expectations, and modified the proposed applications for ~40% (Ayoubi et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about vendor responses to YCharOS data, supported by citation.

claim: The YCharOS study showed that recombinant antibodies on average outperformed both monoclonal and polyclonal antibodies in all the assays used.
source: Finally, this study showed the value of recombinant antibodies, demonstrating that on average they outperformed both monoclonal and polyclonal antibodies in all the assays used.
evidence: This is a finding from the YCharOS study comparing antibody types.

claim: Only Good Antibodies (OGA) was set up in 2023 and is based at the University of Leicester.
source: Set up in 2023, and based at the University of Leicester, the Only Good Antibodies (OGA; Biddle et al., 2024) community works with and helps to promote the YCharOS pipeline.
evidence: This is a historical fact about OGA's founding, supported by citation.

claim: The Structural Genomics Consortium (SGC) began in 2003 with a focus on the determination of protein structures for the human proteome.
source: The Structural Genomics Consortium (SGC) began in 2003 with a focus on the determination of protein structures for the human proteome, and after considerable success in that arena, moved into other areas, including antibody generation and characterization.
evidence: This is a historical fact about the SGC's founding and mission.

claim: Members of the YCharOS team and representatives from ten leading antibody manufacturers recently co-wrote a method article that contains detailed protocols for Western Blots, immunoprecipitation and immunofluorescence.
source: Towards this end, members of the YCharOS team and representatives from ten leading antibody manufacturers recently co-wrote a method article that contains detailed protocols for Western Blots, immunoprecipitation and immunofluorescence (Ayoubi et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ayoubi et al., 2024.

claim: A combination of immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry can be used to speed and improve the characterization of the selectivity and specificity of antibodies at scale.
source: However, a combination of immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry can be used to speed and improve the characterization of the selectivity and specificity of antibodies at scale in this one use (Marcon et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Marcon et al., 2015.

claim: Technologies allowing rapid screening of large libraries for high-affinity, specific recombinant antibodies are generating large numbers of new antibodies, some with affinities better than those obtainable by immunization.
source: In contrast to the limited role that high-throughput assays are likely to play in the characterization of antibodies, technologies allowing rapid screening of large libraries for high-affinity, specific recombinant antibodies are generating large numbers of new antibodies, some with affinities better than those obtainable by immunization (Azevedo Reis Teixeira et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Azevedo Reis Teixeira et al., 2021.

claim: Deep learning models, such as AlphaFold, should enable predictions of the antibody-antigen complex, aid in the identification of the epitope targeted, and help determine if folding, post-translational modifications or other issues may influence the output from use of the antibody.
source: Finally, a role for technology in this field that will likely play increasingly important roles in the future development and optimization of antibodies will come from deep learning models, such as AlphaFold. These models should enable predictions of the antibody-antigen complex, aid in the identification of the epitope targeted, and help determine if folding, post-translational modifications or other issues may influence the output from use of the antibody.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about future applications of AI/deep learning models.

claim: The Journal of Comparative Neurology was among the first to clearly describe both the need for antibody information in manuscripts and the details of how to include it in a methods section.
source: The Journal of Comparative Neurology was among the first to clearly describe both the need for antibody information in manuscripts and the details of how to include it in a methods section (Saper, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Saper, 2005.

claim: The Michael J Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research has made available 200 research tools to date through its Research Tools Program.
source: Partnering with both manufacturers/vendors and academic researchers who are experts in particular targets, MJFF has made available 200 research tools to date (see, for example, Davies et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about MJFF's output, supported by citation.
